Oṃ, salutations to Śambhu, whose body is the nectar of one's own self.
Now,
the *Spandasamdoha*.
Composed by the venerable and eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, the illustrious Ācārya Kṣemarāja.
He whose greatness is immeasurable, who contemplates within his heart the entire universe— from the earth up to Īśvara and Śiva— through various combinations,
and who manifests the diverse plays of creation and dissolution;
Victorious is that one Śiva alone, who possesses vibration and is established in himself. || 1 ||

(1) "Unmeasured" (*akalita*) means that which is not measured; it is impossible to bring it within the scope of measurement, nor is it projected outside its own nature into the sphere of objective quantification (*idantā*). Its majesty (*mahimā*) consists of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), which is the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*) whose essence is the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) that is non-different from the universe. And he who...
The universe, consisting of existence, non-existence, and that which transcends both, from the earth up to Sadāśiva, He impels within the heart—

which is the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*) that is the locus of the foundation of all— by means of various conjunctions, that is, through diverse acts of reflective awareness (*parāmarśana*), without depending at all on such causal materials as the *upādāna* (material cause).

Although it is not distinct from Him, He manifests as if distinct, like a reflection in a mirror. And He who proclaims the fivefold divine acts—creation, withdrawal, manifestation, the establishment of the seed-state, and dissolution—which constitute His manifold play of creation and withdrawal; He alone is [the Lord], according to the established principle.
Although he moves both within and without the manifold expansion of the world-play that is illuminated by him, he remains the very nature of non-duality;

endowed with the power of absolute freedom (svātantrya-śakti) which is non-different from himself, he abides in the state of resting in his own essential nature. Like the ocean, even amidst the surging of the waves of the universe, he remains established in his own unshakable nature, manifesting as the most supreme of all.
Thus [ends the first section]. || 1 ||
The nectar flowing from the ocean of consciousness, which has severed the machinery of exhaustion,
though vibrating within all, is sealed by the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā).
He who, having skillfully opened this [seal], experiences the inner mouth which bestows supreme fullness and bliss—he is the victorious hero, the lord of the Kula. || 2 ||

(1) Having first referred to the Supreme Deity, he then refers to the Non-Supreme Deity with the words "from the ocean of consciousness" (*caitanyābdheḥ*); that is, from the ocean of the nature of Consciousness— which consists of the state of equilibrium between Light and Bliss—
that which is supramundane, characterized by a tendency to flow forth in an uninterrupted succession of streams.
It is the immortal state consisting of the unsurpassed bliss of one's own self, from which the entire array of the afflictions of worldly existence has been uprooted;
and it is that which, by its very nature, is free from the constraints corrupted by dependence on meditation, worship, and so forth for all the seven classes of subjects.

Although it has dawned within, that Reality, having been brought to a state of suppression by the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) which remains unrecognized as the Śāmbhava Seal, is this very nectar that bestows the bliss of unsurpassed,

perfect I-consciousness; and through the proper method— namely, the thorough cultivation of the means beginning with the Śāmbhava, which are manifested by the descent of the power of Supreme Śiva— it is fully realized.
He who, having unsealed it so as to be free from further obstacles, and having opened it with the desire to enjoy it himself—

first withdrawing the expansion of external activity and then, through inward-turnedness, tastes that which is within the mouth [of consciousness] in the abode of the Supreme Power (paraśakti), whose synonym is the Heart of the Yoginī (yoginīhṛdaya)— he is this very hero (vīra).

Having severed the triple bond of the fetters (pāśa), he is victorious, shining intensely as the sovereign lord by virtue of being the cause of the expansion and contraction of the wheel of the Goddess of the Kula instruments (karaṇeśvarīcakra).
[Page 3]
Since the principle of Spanda was unveiled by the great teachers, we possess a certain curiosity regarding its full expansion. (3)
Therein, the very first aphorism is examined;

for the purpose of bringing about the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of the nature of the Great Lord (*maheśvara*), who consists of supreme non-dual light and bliss, the venerable [author] has taught this appropriate hymn, which contains the essence of the entire meaning of the treatise.
The teacher Vasugupta,
by whose opening and closing of the eyes the dissolution and emergence of the universe occur.
We praise that Śaṅkara, the source of the manifestation of the wheel of powers (śakticakra). || 1 ||
We praise Śaṅkara, our own supreme reality, who bestows grace consisting of the recognition of the light of non-dual consciousness— the ultimate bliss free from all afflictions— and who,
having trampled underfoot the limited state of the subject characterized by the body, vital breaths, and so forth— [we praise him].

And yet, just as the worldly nectar (*amṛta*), though shimmering within the milk-ocean, was constrained by the power of destiny (*niyati-śakti*) through its internal concealment, that too was extracted by means of the method of churning and other practices,
and the Lord of all the gods (*sarvadaivata-indra*) tasted it.
Having attained the true state of perfect bliss, he became one who was free from the afflictions of old age, death, and so forth.
(1) It was taught as being of a secret nature;
(2) by the venerable teacher Vasugupta;
(3) for the purpose of manifesting its wonder.
(4) *Upadrava* consists of the manifestation of division.
(5) Regarding the word "we praise" (*stumaḥ*), when there is an expectation for a subject, the word "we" (*vayam*) is to be understood.
[Page 4]
In all states, whether characterized by conceptualization (*vikalpa*) or non-conceptualization (*avikalpa*), we contemplate Him as the supreme excellence.

The use of the plural number is for the purpose of manifesting the non-difference between Him and all the people to be graced who have been made one with Himself. And the word "Him" (*tam*) is used to bring about the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of His unique essential nature. Who is this Śaṅkara? To this he says: "whose unfolding... (*yasyonmeṣa*).

Thus it is said. Here, some have explained that the dissolution and emergence—the destruction and creation—of the universe, of all things, result from the opening and closing (*unmeṣa-nimeṣa*) which consist in the manifestation and concealment of one's own nature (*svarūpa*).
Others did not tolerate this, for instance, because they held that opening and closing are merely occasional.

How could the causes for the occasional destruction and emergence of the world exist in the eternal Lord? Therefore, because the Lord is the cause of the world characterized by the properties of opening and closing, the single power of the Lord is designated by the two terms "unmeṣa" (opening) and "nimeṣa" (closing). Thus, setting aside the correspondence [of these terms with the specific functions],...

They have explained that, as far as possible, the emergence of the world occurs through His opening of the eyes (*unmeṣa*), and its dissolution through their closing (*nimeṣa*). Here too, from the perspective of the teaching on the meaning of the scriptures, since the world is non-different from the nature of Śaṅkara, how could its destruction and emergence possibly be occasional? This being an equal objection, if—

In accordance with the ultimate reality of manifestation (*ābhāsa-paramārtha*), the arising and destruction of the world— which, as an ultimate reality of such manifestation, is non-different from the nature of Śaṅkara—
are held to be nothing other than His very opening and closing of His eyes (*unmeṣa-nimeṣa*).

(1) Because it possesses the nature of attributes consisting in the occasional concealment of its own essential form and the manifestation of that [form], there would follow the consequence of the Lord— who is always of a single form— being non-eternal.
(2) In reality, everything manifesting through the various diversities of the manifold universe...

It consists solely of manifestation; since it has no form outside of manifestation because it is non-existent, nothing at all would appear—this is the meaning. (3) These two indeed consist of the fivefold cosmic acts, whose nature is the sovereignty of Maheśvara, whose essence is supreme light.

Why are appearance (*tathābhāsa*) and ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) not both accepted in the Blessed Lord? Time, too, has manifestation as its essence and is nothing other than that; so how could this wretched thing [time] exist apart from the Blessed Lord, who is the agent of manifestation?

It is the locus of the suspicion of difference. Furthermore, the definition of *unmeṣa* (opening/expansion), namely "of one who is intent upon a single thought" (3.9), is found right here; and according to that, the definition of *nimeṣa* (closing/contraction) is also [implied].
Others maintain that there is no harm even if the sequence is followed as "the concealment of one's own nature, the manifestation of form, and the formless [state] are to be inferred.

Enough with this narrative description; the subject at hand is now stated: "of which there is the unfolding" (*yasyonmeṣa*). Here, although the Supreme Lord is pure and consists of the Great Light, his power of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa-śakti*) is indeed one alone.

Because its nature is a slight vibration of luminosity, it is proclaimed in the Āgamas by infinite names such as *spanda* (vibration), *sphurattā* (throbbing), *ūrmi* (wave), *bala* (power), *udyoga* (exertion), *hṛdaya* (heart), *sāra* (essence), *mālinī*, and *parā*. And although it is one, it simultaneously consists of both unfolding (*unmeṣa*) and closing (*nimeṣa*). To explain:

That which is the state of *nimeṣa* (closing) regarding the group of principles (*tattva-grāma*)— beginning from Sadāśiva and ending with the earth— which was previously created, in relation to its withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), is itself the state of *unmeṣa* (opening) in relation to the distinctions that are about to be created.

And that very state of *nimeṣa*, which consists in the withdrawal of the distinctions previously created, is [the state] of the manifestation of non-difference from Consciousness (*cid-abheda-prathā*).
The ground of unfolding (*unmeṣa*).

Although time—which is animated by the sequence of unfolding and closing (*unmeṣa* and *nimeṣa*)—is liable to give rise to the suspicion of duality because it threads together distinctions, it remains submerged within that [ground] precisely because its ultimate reality consists in the essence of manifestation; thus, it is not at all capable of creating division.
(2) Since the arising of another thought occurs for one who is intent upon a single thought, that should be known as "unmeṣa" (opening); one should recognize it for oneself. || 3-9 ||
(3) Because of the manifestation of the waves— which are essentially the slight throbbing of the universe— within the immovable ocean of consciousness;
(4) that is to say, because of the unfolding of the distinctions such as blue, pleasure, and so forth, which are about to be created.
The state of manifestation (*unmeṣa*) regarding forms is itself the ground of the closing (*nimeṣa*) of the expansion of non-difference from consciousness.

Even the stage of *māyā*, which consists of the prior ground of the desire to see blue and so forth, is indeed the state of manifestation; it is the very form of the closing, which consists in the resting upon the manifestation of yellow that preceded the flashing forth of blue, [and so on for all things].

It is established by one's own self-awareness (*svasaṃvitsiddhā*). Furthermore, this ground of the desire to see (*didṛkṣābhūmi*), although it consists in the unfolding of the nature that threads together the manifestation of "this-ness" (*idantā*) of the blue, is at that very moment also the ultimate reality of the closing (*nimeṣa*) of that very same [blue] whose nature is non-different from the Supreme Lord; for in truth, even within the sphere of *māyā*.
This supreme ground of reflective awareness (*parā vimarśabhūmi*), whose nature consists of the flickering of all powers as characterized by the opening and closing of the eyes,

though it is always manifesting for everyone within its own self, does not achieve firm establishment in consciousness during the state of *māyā*; nevertheless, it becomes manifest therein from time to time.
"In order to make his own nature clearly known, he will become exceedingly enraged...
and so forth. (1.22) etc.
(1) Because the identification with "I" is assumed toward the body, vital breath, and so forth;

(2) the very desire to see (*didṛkṣā*) is the desire to emit (*sisṛkṣā*), which is that same prior stage consisting of will (*icchā-rūpā*), and that itself is *unmeṣa* (the opening); (3) according to the principle that "the supreme state is one of fluidity," it is precisely within *nimeṣa* (closing) and *unmeṣa* (opening), which consist of withdrawal and emission respectively, [that this occurs].
The intention is that all the powers of the universe are contained within [it].
(4) Whether one is extremely angry or exceedingly joyful, or while deliberating "what shall I do?", or while running—whatever state one enters, therein vibration (spanda) is established. || 22 ||
Adopting such a state, he remains there, having formed the resolve: "Whatever this person says to me, I shall certainly do. (23)
Relying upon that [path], both the Moon and the Sun set within the path of Suṣumṇā by way of the upward route,
having abandoned the domain of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
Then, in that great void where the moon and sun have dissolved,
the deluded one becomes awakened and unobscured, like the state of deep sleep.
The four verses ending with "anāvṛtaḥ" (1.25) constitute [the first section]. However,
for one whose veil of *māyā* has been destroyed by the manifestation of the descent of the supreme power (*paraśaktipāta*), these serve as a support for the hand in attaining the state of Śiva.
It indeed bestows the supreme [state] in its fullness at all times, yet it does not manifest [as such]; as he will say:
"When the agitation subsides...
(1.9), and so forth.
...and performs [this], up to the end of (1.10).

Likewise, starting from "the waking state and so forth" (1.3) up to "that exists in the ultimate sense" (1.5). For instance: when, from the first ground of the state of aesthetic resonance (*sāmarasya*) whose nature is Śiva—

If the universe were not established in a state of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) with the self of perfect I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*), being non-existent, how could it be created? When the state consisting of the desire to perceive blue— which is synonymous with the "falling away" of the *tuṭi*—
has arisen, then, in relation to the mere blue, there exists that [state] which consists of the threading together of "this-ness" (*idantā*) concealed by "I-ness" (*ahantā*).
The state of Sadāśiveśvara is thus described; and at that very moment, it is that [state] itself.
(1) When agitation is dissolved, then the supreme state shall be attained. || 9 ||
Then his innate nature, characterized by knowledge and agency, [manifests], whereby he knows and accomplishes everything that he desires. (10)
Even as it extends through the various states such as waking and so forth, which are distinct from it, it never departs from its own essential nature as the perceiver. || 3 ||

The cognitions "I am happy," "I am suffering," and "I am attached," and so forth, clearly occur in something other [than the body], which persists through the various states of happiness and the rest. (4)
Where there is neither suffering nor happiness, neither the grasped nor the grasper,
and even no state of delusion— that exists from the perspective of ultimate reality.

(3) If the universe, established in a state of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) within the first digit known as the Fullness of Ego (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*), had not existed [therein], how could it have been emitted while being non-existent? Therefore, the intention is that the existence of the universe— which is non-different from its own essential nature— must necessarily be admitted prior to creation.
This is clarified for the purpose of making known the nature of the opening of the eyes (*unmeṣa*).
(4) This is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the desire to emit the universe. (5) It is the stage of the initial threading together of the "this-ness" (*idantā*) that is about to be emitted.

In relation to the universe established in the state of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) with the self of full subjectivity (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*), even Śiva-hood [is relative]; for if it were not another [aspect] existing as the nature of the light of Sadāśiva, how could it be emitted at a later time?
Because it is logically impossible for anything other than the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) to be the creator; and this has been established in the *Pratyabhijñā* [Tantra]:
"For the Lord, whose essence is consciousness, projects outward by the power of His will that which was situated within."
"Like a yogi, he should manifest the collection of objects without any material substratum. (1.5.7).
Here too, he will say:
"That in which this entire universe resides as an effect, and from which it has emerged... (1.2).

Thus, these states of Śiva, Sadāśiva, and Īśvara exist as a single form through their mutual pervasion. When this is said, "when that," this sequence exists only in speech from the perspective of the disciple, not in reality. Therefore, this consciousness is simultaneously both creator and destroyer; it appears as having a sequence [only] in its manifestation.
She is the form of both creator and destroyer, consisting of the light of pure *ahantā* (I-consciousness), and is even beyond succession (*akrama*). Enough said.
Only those whose wealth is instruction perceive this ground. And here too, in the sūtra [3.11], "as if out of a desire to see... [the same applies].
As the presiding subject— (1|11)—

the status of being a creator is not possible for anything such as *māyā* or *prakṛti*, which are distinct from the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), because they are struck down by the dilemma of being either different or non-different [from consciousness]. For indeed, if they were separate from the light of consciousness, they would be non-existent due to their lack of manifestation.
But since, in the absence of difference, the nature of consciousness is established by the very fact of its being manifest,

there follows a sequence of description— beginning from the unnameable essential nature and ending with the plane of Śiva and so forth— for the sake of awakening the disciple. In reality, however, the manifestation of the universe is indeed without sequence and consists solely of the supreme reality.
This is the intended meaning.
(3) When [the mind] remains pervading all objects as if out of a desire to see them, then what is the use of much speaking? One will understand for oneself. || 3.11 ||
For one who, beholding that intrinsic nature as the presiding subject, remains as if smiling, how could this deceptive course of action possibly exist? (1-11)
And in this regard, this alone is the intended meaning of the instruction:
"Always for the sake of the sport of emanation..."
"Unresting at every moment"—
and "when there is sovereign power within oneself"—
in such passages, this is precisely the intention of the teachers; and there is also scriptural authority [to support this].
The Goddess is eternally licking [the world], and she shines forever full;
she is this wave of the ocean of consciousness, the Lord’s power whose essence is will.

Thus, this single, undivided ground of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which consists of both unfolding (*unmeṣa*) and closing (*nimeṣa*), is designated by the two terms "unfolding" and "closing. Consequently, having analyzed the compound as "the unfoldings and the closings," [it refers to] the unfolding that consists of closing, and the closing that consists of unfolding.

The state of being the cause of the dissolution and emergence of the universe—divided into primary and secondary [levels] from the earth up to Sadāśiva—must be explained. Furthermore, by analyzing the compound as "both dissolution (*pralaya*) and emergence (*udaya*)," it should be interpreted as *pralayodayau*. For instance, that which is the emergence of the external form of blue and other objects is precisely this [power].

The dissolution of the nature of "I-ness" (ahantārūpatā) is such that the very dissolution of external form is itself the emergence of the nature of "I-ness"; thus, even dissolution is of the nature of emergence, and even emergence has dissolution as its ultimate reality. [This concerns] the non-duality of difference and non-difference...
(1) Homage to the Lord, who always delights in creation, who always dwells in the bliss of maintenance, and who is eternally satisfied by consuming the three worlds.

Thus it is said in the *Stotrāvalī* and in the *Stavacintāmaṇi*: "Victorious is that certain, unborn, and non-conceptual One, who, though incessantly fashioning the three worlds through hundreds of mental constructs at every moment, remains himself free from conceptualization."
The meaning is that even in a state of emaciation, she shines forth as if full.
The distinction here is merely based on the presence or absence of grain; in reality, it is the conscious self (*cidātman*) alone that appears in such a manner.
It has been stated that here there is indeed no sequential order; and in this very way, the compound is justified.
And thus, regarding the *dvandva* compound, the *Bhāṣya* says: "If the intention is to provide an illustration, it is as follows..."

One should point out the *dhava* and *khadira* trees, and so forth. And in this very system of the independent non-dual Śiva, the multiplicity of each individual object is logically consistent; for elsewhere, entities possess fixed forms, such that one [word] has two meanings, and another [word] likewise.

"What is the connection with the phrase 'having two meanings'?"—enough of this irrelevant matter. And since it has been explained in this way, that which is described as the Supreme Lord’s performance of the fivefold activity (*pañcavidhakṛtyakāritva*) in the *Śrīsvacchanda* and other scriptures is also accepted. And thus, by means of the unfolding (*unmeṣa*) consisting of the initial threading of differentiation and its subsequent manifestation...
The creation of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) is twofold, consisting of pure and impure forms, through a slight closing of the essential nature (svarūpa-nimeṣa).
Thus, through that twofold differentiation of closing, there is withdrawal (saṃhāra) in the form of an upward opening (unmeṣaṇa) that touches upon slight non-differentiation.
Likewise, through the two—opening and closing—which have become intermingled (lolībhūta)—[withdrawal occurs].

The ultimate state is the persistence of the flow of both manifestation and non-manifestation; as it has been said: "The supreme state is that which is in a state of constant vibration. This is according to the doctrine that the ultimate reality consists of the nature of light (*prakāśamayatā*), wherein there is but a single reality.
It is traditionally taught that the Self consists of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*) and possesses manifold meanings.
Furthermore, through the opening and closing [of His eyes], the fivefold cosmic activity of the Supreme Lord, beginning with creation, is also accepted.
(3) By "unmeṣa" (expansion), the meaning is by way of both the non-conceptual and conceptual forms;
thus it was stated by the Siddhapādas. Likewise, in reality, [it] consists of the manifestation of the expansion of one's own arisen nature.

The full closing (*nimeṣa*) of one's own essential nature, which consists of the experience of hell and other [lower states], is dissolution (*vilaya*). Furthermore, the full opening (*unmeṣa*) of one's entire being—which, because it pacifies all differentiation, is described as the previously mentioned prosperity—is the closing consisting of grace (*anugraha*). Thus, by this very [process], the Supreme Lord possesses the agency of the fivefold cosmic functions (*pañcakṛtya*).

Touched. In this way, even dissolution (*pralaya*) and emergence (*udaya*) are to be reconciled. Furthermore, dissolution and so forth reside in the manifested object and consist essentially of manifestation; they are nothing at all for this Supreme Lord, whose nature is Light.
As he will say:
And here, the pair of states— beginning from [1-14] "it is"— up to [1-14] "agency"— is established.

Thus far. Even on the level of the illusory subject (*māyā-pramātṛ*), this fivefold performance of ritual acts (*pañcavidha-kṛtya*) remains established for the Supreme Lord, whose nature is light; however, that [fivefold activity] is fully cognizable only by those possessing a consciousness that is attentive to its connection. For such is the Blessed One.
At the time of the manifestation of blue and so forth, there is the state of being the creator (*sraṣṭṛtā*) within the appearance of blue that is permeated by space and time;
when, upon the suspicion of it being permeated by other spaces, times, and forms,
the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) dissolve and all differentiation is destroyed, there remains even the latent impression of that very differentiation which has been destroyed.
Such a one perishes as the very self of full unfolding; yet, within the processes of creation, maintenance, withdrawal, and dissolution,
there remains a mutual residue of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) which, without divine grace, is in reality difficult to sever, for that alone is the cause of transmigratory existence.

(2) And here there is a pair of states designated as "the state of being an effect" and "the state of being an agent. Of these, the state of being an effect is perishable, whereas agency is imperishable.
(3) In this regard, it is understood by those who attend to the relationship between the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*) that [the process] is complete:
[there is] withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), and the state of being the cause of persistence for the general manifestation of blue and so forth prior to creation, in that very [place].
The principle that "in the emission of the non-differentiated aspect, there is the cause of dissolution," and so forth, should also be applied to the appearance of yellow and other such phenomena.

Thus, with respect to the state of blue as it first appears and its corresponding grasper, there is the quality of being the "dissolver" (saṃhartṛtva); with respect to the state of the appearing yellow and its corresponding grasper, there is the quality of being the "emitter" (sṛṣṭṛtva).

In relation to appearances such as those characterized by discontinuity, it is the cause of persistence; in relation to appearances reduced to the form of internal latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), it effects dissolution;
and in relation to appearances whose state as seeds of memory and so forth has been dissolved through their attainment of identity with pure consciousness.

Thus, being the bestower of grace, the fivefold performance of action—which is the very nature of Maheśvara—remains everywhere, expanding as a single form at all times and in all conditions. In that very state, within one's own essential nature, which consists of the sovereignty of consciousness, is the form of Śaṅkara, self-luminous; [this is realized] by some alone.

The intellect of those who possess the wealth of unsurpassed samādhi ascends [to the highest state], but not that of others who conceive of an "I-ness" (ahaṃbhāva) regarding the body and so forth. As it is said in the *Bhargaśikhā*:
"Even the deity Vīrabhairava has a form consisting of supreme bliss."
How could it arise in the hollow of the heart of a beast, which is marked by the mire of delusion?
Thus, the manner of instruction as explained will become clear right here later on:
(1) for one who possesses the cognition of the state of being blue;
(2) for the yellow object being created.
(3) of the object appearing as differentiated;
(4) having attained non-difference from the nature of consciousness;
(5) in reality, it is Maheśvara’s own sovereignty that manifests in five ways through various playful activities such as creation.
The meaning is that it shines forth.
(6) The *ciccakra* is the manifestation of the nature of consciousness (*cit-svarūpa*) as the form of the universe in various ways;
that itself is sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), and Śaṅkara is of that very essence. In that state, rest is attained only by certain yogins.
This is the meaning. [Page 13] Waking and so forth... (1–3)
Beginning with "it exists from the perspective of ultimate reality" up to this point [in verse 1.5],
it is likewise stated here.

The perception of that [reality] is constant and never deviates from the three states. (1.17) Therefore, one who is constantly diligent in the discernment of the principle of Spanda—[he whose consciousness... (2.5) thus.
The awakened one should remain always—[3]—in such places as these; and at the conclusion of the book, he will summarize this very point:
"But when he is firmly established in one [state], then for him there are both dissolution and emergence."
"By restraining [the senses], one attains the state of the enjoyer, and thereby becomes the Lord of the Wheel" (3.19).

For here, dissolution (*laya*) and emergence (*udaya*) are explained as having the supreme reality (*paramārtha*) alone as their object. And this very sovereignty of the wheel (*cakreśvaryam*) consists in being the nature of consciousness that always performs the fivefold cosmic act.
Even though it extends through the various distinctions of waking and so forth, it never departs from its own innate nature as the perceiver, which remains undifferentiated therein. (3)

The cognitions "I am happy," "I am miserable," and "I am attached" clearly persist in something other [than the states themselves], which runs through the various conditions such as happiness and so forth. (4)
Where there is neither suffering nor happiness, neither the grasped object nor the grasper, and even no state of delusion—that exists from the perspective of ultimate reality. (5)
Or, he for whom there is such a realization that the entire world is a play—he who sees thus, being constantly disciplined, is liberated while living; of this there is no doubt. (2.5)
(3) One who is awakened should always remain, having discerned the field of experience through knowledge;
one should unify everything in one place, and thereby one is not oppressed by anything else. 3-2.
(4) Dissolution has arising as its ultimate reality, and arising also has dissolution as its ultimate reality; thus, both are composed of the manifestation of ultimate reality.
Enough with these discourses that merely provide consolation to the hearts of a few people!

Furthermore, it is by the opening and closing— the manifestation and withdrawal— of the Self, which is a mass of consciousness-bliss, that the world exists externally, having been made so from what was within.

The dissolution and emergence—the sinking and surfacing—of that which has the form of the body, and by extension of the external universe as well, should be applied respectively to *samāveśa* (immersion) and *vyutthāna* (emergence).
Now, one might ask: according to the method taught in the venerable *Svacchanda-tantra* and other scriptures, how is it that [the cycles of] Brahmā and the others...

Just as the dissolution and emergence of the worlds situated below [the state of the Lord] occur only as distinct from the states of sleep and waking, so too, in relation to the Supreme Lord, the dissolution and emergence of the universe occur only as something distinct; this much has been stated. For it is observed that potters and others produce effects that are distinct from themselves.

To dispel the doubt as to whether [the Lord] is accepted as established by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) or otherwise, he states the reason by way of a qualification: "arising from the manifestation of the wheel of powers" (*śakticakravibhavaprabhava*). [As it is said:
"His powers are this entire universe, but the Great Lord (*maheśvara*) is the possessor of power."
(1) By this principle, that which exists internally is merely made manifest externally; such is the meaning.

(2) The emergence of the conscious self (*cidātman*) is *samāveśa* (immersion); the emergence of the world is *vyutthāna* (emergence from meditation); and the unfolding of non-duality is the dissolution (*pralaya*) of the world.
(3) Of those residing in the worlds such as the Truth [Realm] (*satyaloka*);
(4) by way of their non-differentiated nature.

According to the established position of the scriptures (*āgama*), whatever appears is entirely nothing but manifestation (*prakāśa*), because it is logically impossible for that which is non-manifest (*aprakāśa*) to be manifested. Furthermore, by the force of reasoning, it is observed in cases such as dreams and mental constructs that consciousness alone is the cause of the emergence of appearances; and this is also in accordance with direct experience (*anubhava*) regarding manifestation itself.

The universe manifesting from the Blessed One is his power (*śakti*); the "wheel" (*cakra*) of those powers is the collection established through the variety of their conjunctions and so forth. That itself is the "manifestation" (*vibhava*), meaning expansion;
it is the "source" (*prabhava*) because [the universe] originates from it—thus, its ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) consists in appearing in such and such ways.

That which is one's very own nature; as he will say: "Because the individual soul (*jīva*) consists of all things and is the source of all states of being, through its identity with them, by virtue of having the form of their consciousness. (2-3)
Thus [it is said]: "Because of identity, there is the cognition of that; for that reason," and so forth.

Alternatively, the "power" (*vibhava*) of the wheel of powers—that is, the group of sense organs—consists in their engagement with their respective objects and so on; the "source" (*prabhava*) of that is as explained previously. For he will state:
For this group of instruments [performs] the activities of manifestation, maintenance, and withdrawal.
He obtains— (1 | 6)—
thus:
(1) the universal aggregate.
(2) Since this group of instruments, though itself deluded, acts as if undeluded,
it performs the functions of manifestation, maintenance, and withdrawal along with the internal wheel.
And furthermore, the source of the power of the wheel of energies (*śakticakra*)— that is, the wheel of the sovereign of the instruments (*karaṇeśvarīcakra*)—
is its capacity to perform the manifold acts of creation, withdrawal, and so forth.
It consists of the great non-successive light, produced by its function of manifesting the succession of objects; as he will say:
"Together with the internal wheel, it performs the functions of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal."
"Obtains... (1.6).

Thus, it is this very internal wheel (*cakram*) that must be explained here, and not the triad of internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇatrayam*), because the latter has already been subsumed within the category of the instruments (*karaṇavarga*). The category of the instruments consists merely of the activity (*pravṛtti*) and so forth of one's own self.

It should be explained that for the wheel of the Mistress of the Organs (*karaṇeśvarīcakra*), the very performance of creation and so forth constitutes the attainment of activity and the rest; enough of this.
The "wheel of power" (*śakticakra*) refers to the collection of mantras and the multitude of mudrās; its "majesty" (*vibhava*) is as follows.
The capacity to accomplish the threefold success (*siddhi*) is its "source" (*prabhava*); that is, the place of rest for its arising, characterized as a source. As he will say:
"Having ascended that power, the mantras... (2.1).
...and so forth,
up to the end of [the passage] "the stainless ones" (2.2).
And by means of the power of the manifestation of the wheel of energies (*śakticakra*) which has been explained, the mantras...

(1) Of the class of the power of the instruments (*karaṇa-śakti-varga*); (2) the multitude of supreme and non-supreme mantras and mudrās is to be understood from the *Śivasūtra*s and other texts; (3) accomplishment (*siddhi*) is threefold, consisting of the supreme (*parā*), the supreme-non-supreme (*parāparā*), and the non-supreme (*aparā*).
(4) Having taken hold of that power, the mantras, endowed with the power of the Omniscient One,
proceed toward their respective functions, just as the sense organs do for embodied beings.
Right there they dissolve away, tranquil in form and stainless.
[Page 17] That practitioner’s mind, whose radiance and brilliance possess the nature of the power of the directions— that [mind] goes forth.
That which attains, presides over, perfumes, destroys, and comes to rest within itself— this [will become clear] together with the mind of the worshipper. (2.2)
Thus,

the "origin" (prabhava) refers to the source of that teacher whose manifestation occurs through the perfection of power— consisting of the wheel of powers (śakticakra), initiation (dīkṣā), grace (anugraha), meditative object (dhyeya), meditative absorption (samāpatti), and so forth— as he will describe.
"This alone is its arising" [3]—
and so forth—
"[she who bestows the true being of Śiva]" [2.7].
Thus far.
Furthermore, the powers (śaktayaḥ) are the goddesses beginning with Brāhmī, as well as the lineage of causes beginning with Brahmā;
the wheel (cakra) belonging to them [is revealed] to the bound subject (paśu-pramātṛ), whose own nature is empty.

Those who possess the nature of Śiva are those who, while unable to ascend to the higher levels of non-dual form, are adept at moving along the lower paths consisting of duality, together with the minds of their practitioners.
(2) Identity with the deity who is to be meditated upon as one's own self;
(3) this alone is the arising of that object of meditation within the mind of the meditator:
namely, the attainment of identity with it for the practitioner who so desires.
This alone is the attainment of the nectar of immortality; this alone is the grasping of the Self;
and this is the initiation into Nirvāṇa, which bestows the true being of Śiva.
(4) They have as their essence the respective designations beginning with *ka* and ending with *kṣa*.
(5) Of the bound soul (*paśu*) who has forgotten the nature of consciousness.
[Page 18]
The *vyūha* (manifestation), its *vibhava* (pervasive power), and its *prabhava* (origination)—that is, its capacity to produce effects accordingly—as he will state:
"Of the group of powers arising from the mass of sounds... (3.13).
This begins with "ityādi" and ends with "bandhayitrī" (3.16).
"Arising as the subtle elements alone...
[3.17], and so forth, we shall explain in detail. [3.18]

And so on up to that point. The "manifestation" (*vibhava*) of that very wheel of powers (*śakticakra*) is its capacity for ascending higher and higher by abandoning each successive lower level of manifestation in relation to the state of its own essential nature (*svasvabhāvapada*). Its "origin" (*prabhava*) is also to be understood as before. As he will say in this very context:
Established in her own path, she is known as the bringer of accomplishment.
(3.16) (1) Her nature consists in the activity of expanding and descending through determinations (*adhyavasāya*) and so forth that are composed of differentiation (*bheda*).
(2) She renders the group of powers (*śakti-varga*) arising from the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*) into an object of enjoyment.
Having lost his power through the loss of his creative energy (kalā), he is considered a bound soul (paśu) who has gone [astray].
The loss of the supreme nectar-essence for him arises from that which is produced by conditions;
through that, he falls into a state of lack of autonomy, and that [loss] has the subtle elements as its object.
And its powers for veiling its own true nature are perpetually active,
because the arising of cognition does not occur without the interpenetration of words.
This very power, whose nature is action, belonging to Śiva and residing within the bound soul (paśu),
is the binder—
[acting] through the form of the emergence of the subtle elements (tanmātras), which reside in the mind, ego, and intellect.
Constrained by the city of eight, it experiences that which arises from the resulting cognitions.
Under the sway of another, he experiences enjoyment; because of that state, he wanders through saṃsāra.
Therefore, we shall explain the cause of this saṃsāra and its dissolution.

...thus [it is said]. Furthermore, the "wheel of powers" (*śakticakra*) refers to the multitude of various *yoginīs*—such as the *Khecarī*, *Gocarī*, *Dikcarī*, and *Bhūcarī*—distinguished by the divisions of external and internal states, as well as the host of heroes (*vīra*) characterized by them. Of that [wheel]...
That which is *vibhava*—

which fulfills and completes sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) consisting in the attainment of infinite minor and major supernatural powers (*siddhi*), such as the knowledge of the past and future, the attainment of the *aṇimā* and other [eight yogic powers], the enjoyment of one's own objects, and the acquisition of the full expansion of time— is that which attains it.
And he is that very Bhava, because he manifests as that particular manifestation through various forms;
as he will say in the *Vibhūtispanda*:
"The Creator, when entreated according to one's desire... [2] (3.1).
By such [reasoning],
how could that [causal power] be causeless? (3.8) A collection of those possessing powers, characterized by a wheel of powers, cannot exist without one who possesses those powers.
Because stability is untenable:
(2) Just as the Creator, when requested by his own will, brings about for embodied beings the rising of the moon and sun so that they may attain the objects situated within their hearts while awake.
Likewise, because it never fails to fulfill desired objects even in dreams,
that which abides in the center must necessarily manifest with extreme clarity.
Otherwise, however, creation would be independent because it would possess that nature [of being self-sufficient],
just as in the two states of waking and dreaming for an ordinary person.
For just as an object seen indistinctly, even when the mind is attentive, appears much more clearly later on when cultivated through the exertion of its own power; so too is the case here.
Thus, whatever exists in its ultimate sense, at whatever time, in whatever place, and in whatever manner— that very thing proceeds forth before long, having been taken hold of by power.
For even one who is weak proceeds toward his task by overcoming it;
likewise, one who is excessively hungry should conceal his hunger.
Just as omniscience and other qualities [arise] when the body is presided over by this [wisdom],
so too will it be everywhere through presiding over one's own self.
Illness is a plunderer of the body, and its course arises from ignorance;
if that [ignorance] is destroyed by the unfolding of [true] consciousness, how could it exist without a cause?

By these eight verses ending on page 20, the internal and external wheels (*cakras*) presided over by Śrī Vāmeśvarī— namely Khecarī, Gocarī, Dikcarī, and Bhūcarī— are explained, wherein [the powers] flow forth.

The universe consists of both difference and non-difference, yet its essence is difference; they loudly proclaim this, they utter it as having difference for its core, and they bring about that which consists of both difference and non-difference so that its essence becomes non-difference—thus, the "Vāmas" (the Left-handed) powers are those whose conduct is contrary to worldly norms. Their sole sovereign and mistress is the Blessed Lady, for the universe is presided over by her.

The left wheel (*vāmācakra*) is also designated as the wheel of Vāmeśvarī. They are called *khecaryah* because they move in the sky (*khe*), which is the space of consciousness; they abide on the plane of the subject (*pramātṛbhūmi*) and consist essentially in the emission of the expansion of conscious bliss for those purified by the descent of the supreme power (*paraśaktipāta*).

Because they are not delimited by time, their ultimate realities consist in the unfolding of one's own nature as non-dual, all-pervasive creatorship, omniscience, fullness, and omnipresence; however, for those deluded by *māyā*, they are the bestowers of non-bliss, moving within the ground of the void subject (*śūnyapramātṛ*), namely: Time (*kāla*), Limited Agency (*kalā*), Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), Attachment (*rāga*), [and so forth].

They are "bondage-makers" because they consist of necessity (*niyati*). They are called *gocaryas* because they "move within" (*caranti*) speech (*gauḥ*), which is indicative of the planes of intellect, ego, and mind that consist of discursive thought (*saṃjalpamayi*). For those who have received the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), these [powers] cause the growth of pure resolve, self-identification, and intention; for others, however, they produce the opposite.

They move within the ten directions and the spheres of the external senses; thus they are "those who move in the directions" (*dikcaryāḥ*). For those who have been graced, their essence consists in the manifestation of non-duality, whereas for others, they fall into the perception of duality. *Bhūḥ* (the ground) is the sphere of the object of cognition (*meyapada*), consisting of the fivefold [objects] beginning with form (*rūpa*); therein they move.

(1) Because they are presided over by the Lord, the powers known as Vāmā and the others residing therein produce a corresponding capacity; (2) because they are perceived as non-different from His own power.
(3) Of the contracted subjects who have been brought to the manifestation of duality by the supreme power of the Lord known as Māyā.
[page 21]
Then, through the process of solidification (*āśyānībhāva*) arising from that very expansion (*ābhoga*), those who move upon the earth attain identity with that [expansion];

they manifest for the awakened as the body of the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa-śarīra*), while for others, they appear as the delimiters of all things. Thus, they are extended by the power of Vāmeśvarī.

The four internal wheels— Khecarī, Gocarī, Bhūcarī, and Dikcarī— are so designated because they are the causes for the manifestation of the states of the "not-terrible," the "terrible," and the "most terrible" (aghoraghoraghoratara), and they are accompanied by such hosts of Vīras.
As it is said in the Śrīpūrvaśāstra:

Still others are known as the most terrible (ghoratara), who, having embraced the rudra-entities, cause the subtle souls (aṇu) who are utterly absorbed in sense objects to fall further and further downward.
Those [impurities] which, as before, produce attachment to the fruits of mixed karma and obstruct the path to liberation, are the terrible *parāpara* [impurities].
As before, those supreme Aghora Śiva-powers, which bestow the fruit of the abode of Śiva upon the multitude of living beings, have been described by the knowers of that [reality].

Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, these external [powers] are indeed presided over by Vāmeśvarī; they are the wheels (cakras) of the Khecarīs, Bhūcarīs, Gocarīs, and Dikcarīs. Among them, the Khecarīs move in the sky and are bodiless;
from the mere will of which arises the awakening of pure knowledge (śuddhavidyā) born from the union of the couple presided over [by her].
He is born from the womb of the Yoginīs. As it is said in the *Śrītantrāloka*:
"And other gurus and their wives, arisen from the lineage of the venerable Kālī, possessing infinite bodies, sport with various unhesitating forms."
When the will to awaken [the consciousness] arises, that which is born from it—the Kaula—shines forth.
(1) The *vīras* are those possessed of power (*śaktimantaḥ*).
(2) Or, they are *rudras* because they cause the bound souls (*paśus*) to weep by casting them down, or because they dissolve the affliction of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra-ruj*).

(3) The grammatical connection is as follows: those supreme and intermediate powers (*parāpara-śakti*) which produce attachment to actions that are mixed with the pursuit of enjoyment and liberation, and which obstruct the path to liberation, are called "terrible" (*ghora*).

Thus: the *gocaryas* are those devoted to extracting the essence from the hearts of the sacrificial animals (*paśu*) denoted by the word "cow" (*go*), and by that very sequence, they are intent upon the means for attaining various supernatural powers (*siddhi*) for themselves and for other animals; they seize these animals from one birth up to as many as seven births. The *dikcaryas*, however, [wander] everywhere like a revolving wheel.

Moving toward the attainment of both the supreme and the lower, the *bhūcarīs* (earth-dwellers) arise by their very own nature from specific regions such as Kuṅkuma, Nārikela, and so forth, born of those various yellow and other lands;
they emerge as portions of those respective deities, distinguished by various qualities such as fullness and non-fullness.
Moreover, regarding the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*),
which is the ultimate reality of various deities well-known through the tradition of the scriptures (*āgama-sampradāya*),
and likewise the entire collection of mental states such as passion, hatred, anger, and conceptual construction; thus:

The "source" (prabhava) refers to both: the manifestation (*vibhava*)—the specific power established by various Upaniṣads—of the multitude of elements and so forth, which constitute the ultimate reality of the respective deities residing in the body; and its state of being an obstacle for those deluded by *māyā*. He will teach this very point.
"The outflows of the vibration of the qualities and so forth arise from the reliance upon the universal vibration" (1.19),
and so on,
up to "on the path of saṃsāra" (1.20).
Thus far. Likewise, [it is said] in [the passage beginning]: "In this way, this very power, whose nature is action, belongs to Śiva" (3.16), and so forth.
It is also stated elsewhere in the Āgamas.
(1) Saffron grows on yellow soil, and it is well known that the coconut tree grows on the uppermost part of the earth.
(2) Movements and non-movements arising from qualities and so forth, having attained their own existence by relying upon the universal movement (*sāmānyaspanda*),
shall never be obstacles for the knower.
But those of unawakened intellect, striving to conceal their own true state,
cast others onto the terrible path of saṃsāra, which is so difficult to cross.
Those who, not knowing the essence of the *kula*, fall into duality,
being blinded by the conceptual constructions arising from their own minds, fall into hell.
Thus:
"By whatever fierce karma sentient beings are bound,
by that very same means they are liberated from the bondage of existence."

Thus, an exposition of this kind is in agreement with various scriptures; however, it has not been written here for fear of making the book too voluminous, and it can be followed by those who have themselves been purified by the descent of the supreme power (*para-śaktipāta*). For others, even if this were demonstrated through hundreds of scriptural citations, [it would remain incomprehensible].
In reality, it does not remain for even a moment, like a drop of water fallen upon a stone slab heated by the summer sun; enough of this.
Furthermore, [it refers to] the multitude of rays belonging to the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*), which effect entry into one's own great light that is autonomous and non-dual.
A slight radiance, which brings satisfaction to the heart as it is manifested through the power of its own unfolding fragrance,

consists of the manifestation of *bindu*, *nāda*, and so forth— accomplished effortlessly by the mere support of its own nature even when attained through the limited efforts of yogis— and serves as a source of agitation.
When this [state] arises for the person of knowledge, it weaves— that is, it brings about— the continuous thread of the realization of the unsurpassed non-dual [consciousness].
From that which he will expand upon,
there is first the *bindu*, and from that, the *nāda*.
And so forth.
(3.10) — "By virtue of being the agitator of embodied beings.
(1) The very essence consists in the thorough knowledge of the *kulas*—such as the body, the senses, the worlds, and so on—as being of the nature of power (*śakti*).
(2) From this [state] arises the drop (*bindu*), from that the sound (*nāda*), from that form (*rūpa*), and from that the flavor (*rasa*);
these emerge very swiftly as the agitators of embodied beings.

...up to this point (page 24). We praise Śaṅkara, who is of such a nature, whose own essential being (*svasvabhāva*) is the source of the manifestation of the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*), and whose form has been explained. Thus, by this—

By means of this portion of the verse, which contains the introduction of the present subject, it has been established that Śaṅkara is his own essential nature— both transcending the universe and consisting of the universe— according to the direction of the teachings of the Trika and other traditions of the Uttamākulā;
however, it is not of the same tenor as the Vedāntins, who hold that the universe is not Brahman itself.
"Non-existence does not become an object of cultivation...
(1.12), and so forth;
however, being remembered in this way does not establish that as the true reality (tattva). (1.13)

This is because [the text] negates [this view] with the words "it ends thus. Nor is it of the nature that the supreme reality is transcendent to the universe alone, as seen in the Siddhānta [view], for [it states]:
"Its perception is constant and never deviates from the three states" (1.17).

Because this would result in contradictions such as those mentioned above; nor is its nature like that of the *aprakaṭita-ākula-svarūpa-kula-prakriyā* scriptures, which hold that the full form consists of the universe itself. As it is said: "When agitation (*kṣobha*) dissolves, then there is the supreme state" (1.9).

Because of such inconsistencies as these; having thus reflected upon the entire meaning of the scriptures through the unity of their statements, one should always, in all states, remain established in the firm realization of one's own true nature as Śaṅkara.
Not even the slightest contempt should be shown toward this [teaching]. However, it is solely for the sake of removing nescience (*akhyāti*) that...
Effort must always be maintained; it is taught that there is no state in which Śiva-nature does not manifest.
As commanded by the Supreme Lord in the *Śrī-svacchanda* and other scriptures:
"Wherever the mind may dissolve, one should contemplate right there."
Having moved, where will it go, since everything is composed of Śiva?
(1) Non-existence does not become something that can be cultivated, nor is there freedom from delusion regarding it;
for, through contact with diligent application, there arises the certainty: "It existed [in the past]."
Therefore, that [state] should always be known as artificial, like the state of deep sleep;
for such a state of being remembered does not attain the status of that true reality.
Thus [it is said]. Here too, he will state:
"There is no state that is not Śiva" (2.4).
And so forth. There is also a *Śivasūtra*:
"This Self is once and for all luminous; there is no possibility whatsoever of its being non-luminous.
Likewise:

"By [the words] 'The universe is the plenum of consciousness, full of the Self,' and so forth"— thus has been explained this first aphorism, which is exceedingly clear yet profound, and which serves as the supreme summary of the essential meaning of the entire scripture. May it [grant its fruit].
May there be auspiciousness for all.
Having grasped merely a fraction of the meaning of the ocean of the Śāstra, some of limited intellect are satisfied;
others, despite their extensive efforts, do not reach its further shore at all; yet others float about halfway like blades of grass, while still others sink and surface again and again.
Others, however, are weary of leading all this; yet even these lords have vomited it up for the sake of those who seek it. || 1 ||
When that [state] comes within the range of mindfulness, the continuous bonds of fetters,
with their internal knots suddenly unraveled, fall apart;
and there flows a stream distilling the bliss of the moon of consciousness.
We take refuge in that auspicious one, who is sprinkled with the nectar of immortality. || 2 ||

Having heard this correctly from my new Lord— the Guru whose light pierces through all darkness, who is like the cool-rayed moon in the ocean of knowledge, and who effortlessly liberates the infinite multitude of supplicants with a mere glance— and having remembered a little of it myself...
For the sake of those who seek it, this *Śrīspandasūtra* has been briefly unveiled by Kṣema for the benefit of seekers. || 3 ||
Thus ends the Spandasamdoha.
This is the work of Rājānaka Kṣemarāja, who lives in dependence upon the lotus feet of the venerable Abhinavagupta, the preeminent teacher of the Great Śaiva tradition.
When the assembly of texts and learned scholars— the refuge of the six sciences—
had undergone decline due to the passage of time;

[This was composed] for the sake of his professional activity by one endowed with the vigor of true discernment, whose mind is solely intent upon the desire to uphold each respective True Dharma. || 1 ||
Having deliberated with his principal ministers who were devoted to righteousness, the illustrious sovereign of Kaśmīra established [this work],
which is pregnant with spiritual knowledge and realized wisdom.
That which is the primary office for the extraction of texts. || 2 ||
May this work, having been refined by the virtuous who enter upon the way of livelihood (ājīva) under the supervision of Mukunda and Rāma,
be perfected through completion, purity, and exposition.
This complete work is for the welfare of virtuous people. || 3 ||
The forehead mark.
May it be offered to the illustrious Śiva.
